newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gencor plans debut on world stage.
newsitem.headline: Gencor plans debut on world stage.

text.p: Mining house Gencor Ltd is poised to group and list its base metals interests in London, returning another South African giant to the international business arena, analysts said on Monday.

Gencor's announcement earlier that it was considering accessing international markets to help fund future projects is part of a trend, embarked on by the country's mining houses to compete with their Australian and North American rivals.

Moving abroad would most likely take the form of a listing of Gencor's offshore arm Billiton International as a base metals company and maintain Gencor Ltd as a listed precious metals company in South Africa, analysts said.
Grouping aluminium, nickel, cobalt and copper interests and listing them on the London Stock Exchange as Billiton could win for Gencor an internationally recognised rating, analysts said.

"The Billiton name might be quite useful. It's partly recognition, partly rating. This would depend on whether they can transform the Gencor rating into the Billiton structure," said Trevor Pearton at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak.
This would draw investors into the offshore-listed share and open doors to raise capital, allowing Gencor more flexibility to move into projects worldwide, analysts said.

"Gencor is currently evaluating a number of major opportunities, including projects in South Africa and Mozambique, in Venezuela and Brazil, and in Colombia and Australia," the company said in a statement.

"Although it is likely that not all of these will advance beyond the study phase, it is clear that Gencor's ability to compete for and finance such projects would be significantly enhanced if it did not have to rely solely on its domestic capital market."
This followed a report by Britain's Observer newspaper on Sunday that Gencor planned to float a new mining operation in London which could be worth up to one billion pounds.

"They want to split off the gold side from the non-gold side and it would make sense to list Billiton, or a separate company under Billiton," said Angus Auchterlonie, analyst at Mathison and Hollidge.
A London listing would be the most sensible because of a common language and the size of the bourse, analysts said.
But they added that one of the key hurdles -- indicated by Gencor -- to achieving this was the lifting of South Africa's foreign exchange controls.

South African companies are barred from having more than 10 percent of their assets abroad. Giant Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd overcame this obstacle during the apartheid era by forming an exclusively offshore company Minorco SA, registered in Luxembourg.
Talk of listing a separate base metals company has been doing the market rounds for a number of years since Gencor first acquired its Dutch subsidiary Billiton in 1994.
Traditionally a gold mining house, Gencor has over the last few years ventured successfully into base metal operations.

Listing speculation gathered momentum when the group announced last year it had lifted its stake in local aluminium company Alusaf to 100 percent. Analysts said at the time Gencor might join its local aluminium interests with those of Billiton.
Lately Gencor has gained control of Colombia's Cerro Matoso nickel mine and is eyeing nickel and cobalt deposits in Cuba.

"They're (Gencor) a focused operator. They don't have universal coverage. They're looking for specific niches. They're not emotionally tied to metals and places. They look purely at strategy and performance," Pearton said.
